From 587 µs to 83 µs

Lecture 01 · The question

What are we actually optimizing?

We are not optimizing “a matrix multiply” in the abstract. We are arranging data, work, and dependencies so that 256 compute units can continuously issue scaled MFMA instructions without waiting on memory, LDS ownership, synchronization, or spilled registers.

C[M,N] = dequantize(AMXFP4, SA) × dequantize(BMXFP4, SB)T
A

Activation operand

Packed E2M1 values: two 4-bit elements per byte.

B

Weight operand

Packed E2M1 rows; the public TLX path accepts raw B.

SCALE

Block scaling

One E8M0 scale for every 32 logical K elements.

C

Output

FP32 accumulation narrowed to BF16 at the epilogue.

The starting point was facebookexperimental/triton PR #2569. It supplied a bit-exact AITER comparison and showed a large gap between tuned assembly and the original TLX paths. Our job was to explain the gap at each compiler layer and recover it without deleting synchronization that carries real correctness dependencies.

Lecture 02 · Feynman model

A restaurant with 256 kitchens

🍳

The GPU is not one fast cook

Think of gfx950 as 256 kitchens. A tile is an order. If a kernel produces only 32 orders, most kitchens are idle. Split-K creates more orders, but also creates partial dishes that must be carried to a second station and combined. Smaller native tiles often fill the kitchens without that cleanup bill.

🧺

LDS buffers are ingredient baskets

Two baskets let the cook consume one while a runner fills the other. Four baskets increase the distance before a basket is reused, giving memory more time to arrive. But every extra basket consumes LDS and registers; deeper is useful only when the loop is long enough and occupancy does not fall.

🧾

Registers are countertop space

AGPRs hold accumulated dishes; VGPRs hold addresses, operands, scales, and temporary work. A 256×256 tile placed two large accumulator halves and too much surrounding work on the counter simultaneously. When the counter overflowed, LLVM put ingredients in “the basement”—scratch memory—and performance collapsed.

Feynman check: If an optimization cannot be explained as “more kitchens working,” “ingredients arriving earlier,” “fewer unnecessary trips,” or “less countertop overflow,” we probably do not understand it yet.
Lecture 03 · The machine

The five-stage journey of one K tile

HBMraw packed A/B + scales
Async copybuffer load to local
LDSswizzled shared tile
Registersdot operands + scales
MFMAFP32 accumulator

VMEM

Moves packed operands from HBM. Useful work requires enough independent requests and legal vector widths.

LDS

A software-managed rendezvous. Fast, but physical ownership, reuse, barriers, and bank behavior are visible to the kernel.

MFMA

v_mfma_scale_f32_* consumes packed FP4 values and scales, accumulating into FP32 VGPR/AGPR state.

Why waits and barriers are different

A wait says, “my asynchronous memory operation has progressed far enough.” A barrier says, “all waves agree that a shared LDS phase is complete.” Removing either blindly can let one wave overwrite a basket another wave is still consuming. Several apparently faster barrier-deletion experiments were nondeterministically wrong.

Lecture 05 · Optimization I

Match the tile to the amount of work

A large tile reduces duplicated loads, but it also reduces the number of independent CTAs. The selector therefore asks how many 256×256 output tiles exist before choosing a kernel family.

grid256×256 = ceil(M/256) × ceil(N/256)
≤ 64 CTAsNative skinny family
32/64/128 × 128
65–255 CTAsFour-wave
128 × 256
≥ 256 CTAsFour-wave
256 × 256
tile benefit = less repeated data work  —  occupancy cost = fewer independent CTAs

The 128×256 layout was derived by removing only the M=128 basis from the proven 256×256 physical layout. That matters: changing logical dimensions without consistently changing lane, warp, shared, accumulator, and store ownership is an invitation to silent data-layout bugs.

Physical layout projectionShape:Stride notation
# 256×256 A-load ownership
shape  = ((8, 8, 4), (16, 4, 2))
stride = ((16, 2048, 128), (1, 512, 16384))

# 128×256: remove the basis that contributes the upper M half
shape  = ((8, 8, 4), (16, 4))
stride = ((16, 2048, 128), (1, 512))
Lecture 06 · Optimization II

Small M needs native ownership

Masking a large tile down to 32 or 64 useful rows still pays for a large ownership pattern. The accepted solution represents those shapes directly.

32×128

Narrow specialization

At 256×4096×4096, it creates exactly 256 CTAs without split-K. Elsewhere it repeats too much B work.

64×128

Small-M workhorse

Four waves, enough output tiles to fill gfx950, and shape-specific two- or four-buffer operand rings.

128×128

Full-grid fallback

Used where the larger skinny tile already exposes enough parallel work and duplication would dominate.

Why split-K is not free occupancy

split-K gain = more compute CTAs  —  FP32 workspace stores  —  reduction launch/read/write

The selector chooses a native tile first, then adds split-K only until the compute grid reaches the measured occupancy target and only when each split retains a viable K loop. Naturally full grids remain SPLIT_K=1.

Four buffers: create distance, not decoration

Source-level unrolling over two LDS objects still reuses those same two objects. Four actual allocations create four distinct SSA/LDS destinations, extending the true overwrite distance.

Conceptual TTGIRfour physical stages
// Prologue: four distinct destinations
amdg.buffer_load_to_local ... into %a_lds_0
amdg.buffer_load_to_local ... into %a_lds_1
amdg.buffer_load_to_local ... into %a_lds_2
amdg.buffer_load_to_local ... into %a_lds_3

scf.for %k = ... step 4 {
  ttg.async_wait {num = 3}
  // consume stage 0; refill it with K+4
  ... repeat for stages 1, 2, 3 ...
}

At the favorable 64×128 full-grid shapes, deeper buffering preserved one four-wave CTA per CU and reduced LDS-read/MFMA dependency stalls. A three-buffer experiment caused a GPU memory fault because the async group/slot reuse schedule was not legal for an odd ring depth.

Lecture 07 · Optimization III

Logical shape is not physical ownership

TLX layouts answer a concrete question: which register, lane, warp, and CTA owns each logical element? This is more precise than saying “row-major” or “contiguous.”

Contiguity

The number of consecutive elements a thread owns for a load. It enables legal wide memory operations. It does not claim that a gather-shaped logical tensor is globally contiguous.

Divisibility / alignment

A promise about pointer values or offsets. It is separate from adjacency. Confusing the two can make a hint invalid even when neighboring elements happen to be consecutive.

Pinned layout through a helpercompiler correctness finding
%offset = ... : tensor<4x256xi32, #physical_linear>
%value = amdg.buffer_load %src[%offset] {contiguity = 4}
    : tensor<4x256xf8E4M3FN, #physical_linear>

// Restructuring the loaded value must not release %offset ownership.
%r0 = tt.reshape %value ...
%r1 = tt.trans %r0 ...

The small-M AITER-shaped experiment exposed a helper-boundary bug: reshape/trans/split/join in a helper could release all pinned arguments, even when the pinned offset itself never flowed through that transformation. The fix performs per-argument SSA-flow analysis and treats loads, stores, dots, and calls as ownership boundaries.

Compiler principle: layout propagation must follow the value that changes shape, not erase physical promises merely because a neighboring value is transformed.
Lecture 08 · Optimization IV

Move scales directly to LDS

The earlier scale path materialized a global load in registers and then stored it to LDS. The optimized path makes scales part of the direct asynchronous copy pipeline.

Beforeextra register stage
global load scales
        ↓
temporary VGPR values
        ↓
local store to LDS
        ↓
local load for MFMA
Afterdirect async destination
amdg.buffer_load_to_local
        ↓
scale LDS ring
        ↓
local load for MFMA

temporary VGPR stage removed

At long K on the 128×256 path, this reduced intermediate register-to-LDS work and joined scales to the same wait-group structure as A and B. At K=4096, the larger LDS footprint was a small regression, so the compact register-staged scale path remains selected there. One policy does not need to fit every shape.

Lecture 09 · Optimization V

The 256×256 kernel was correct—and catastrophically scheduled

The merged investigation found a striking result: TTGIR and LLVM IR computation were essentially unchanged, yet one LLVM function attribute moved runtime from hundreds of microseconds back to the expected range.

iterative-ilp

256 VGPR + 256 AGPR, 848 B scratch/thread, roughly 130 spill stores and 134 reloads, 294–587 µs.

max-memory-clause

256 VGPR + 220 AGPR, zero scratch, zero spill/reload instructions, 48–83 µs.

LLVM IR: the meaningful pre-RA differenceper-function policy
- "amdgpu-sched-strategy"="iterative-ilp"
+ "amdgpu-sched-strategy"="max-memory-clause"
AMDGPU metadata and ISAbefore → after
; NumVgprs:      256
; NumAgprs:      256
; TotalNumVgprs: 512
; ScratchSize:   848
scratch_store_dword ... ; Folded Spill
scratch_load_dword  ... ; Folded Reload

; NumVgprs:      256
; NumAgprs:      220
; TotalNumVgprs: 476
; ScratchSize:   0
; no scratch_load / scratch_store
🪑

Why can scheduling change register allocation?

Imagine asking every guest to arrive early and leave late: more chairs are needed simultaneously. Instruction scheduling changes where values are born and when their last use occurs. The ILP schedule overlapped too many memory temporaries with two 128-column accumulator halves. The memory-clause schedule bounded those live ranges, so the same calculation fit on-chip.

One compiler, different kernel policies

This fix does not require another LLVM build. The scheduler strategy is attached per function. The unified compiler emits the best measured policy for skinny, 128×256, and 256×256 specializations from one installation.

Lecture 10 · Controlled negative result

Pre-shuffling B is useful—but not magic

AITER accepts pre-shuffled B and scales. We reproduced the weight permutation and exposed it through a separate cached-weight ABI rather than silently changing the raw API.

Physical packed-B slabmetadata-only LDS view
[8, 2048]
  → reshape   [8, 4, 2, 16, 16]
  → transpose [8, 16, 4, 2, 16]
  → reshape   [128, 128]
  → local_trans for the MFMA operand

For M=256, packed B improved TLX by about 1–2%. For M=512 it was neutral or slightly slower. On medium and large kernels it usually moved performance by less than 1.5% and did not remove a load, LDS stage, barrier, or MFMA. Therefore:

  • Small-M packed B remains an explicit opt-in ABI for cached weights.
  • Raw B remains the public default and the basis of the unified 13-shape table.
  • Pre-shuffled B-scales were rejected: direct loads landed on the MFMA critical path and regressed to roughly 22 µs.
  • The large BM256 spill existed before packing; packed B merely enlarged the existing spill frame.
Lesson: A permutation helps only if it removes work or relocates a dependency. A different address sequence with the same instruction families is usually a small, shape-dependent effect.

Published PR baseline versus local AITER

The AITER binary available locally is slower than the AITER numbers printed in PR #2569 on several small shapes. Against those published values, TLX remains 9–16% behind on representative small-M cases. GPU selection did not explain the difference, and the PR does not publish the loaded .co hashes or complete environment. Both facts belong in the conclusion.

Lecture 12 · Scientific method

What did not work—and why that matters

ExperimentOutcomeWhat it taught us
Delete barriersNondeterministicSome barriers protect real LDS overwrite dependencies.
Three-buffer ringGPU memory faultThe existing async group/slot schedule is not odd-depth safe.
Four buffers everywhereShape regressionsReuse distance helps only if resource pressure and loop length permit it.
Force MFMA16Materially slowerMatching AITER's instruction does not match its operand pipeline.
Four-wave AITER-shaped cloneStill ~26 vs ~21 µsExcess waits/barriers remain even after occupancy and instruction count match.
Generic scheduling groupsRegressedThey introduced just-in-time lgkmcnt(0) waits.
Pre-shuffle B at mid/large M−1.5% to +0.8%No pipeline stage or instruction family was removed.
Pre-shuffle B-scales~22 µsDirect scale loads moved onto the MFMA critical path.
iterative-minreg for BM256~160 µsA promising name is not a resource proof; inspect the ISA.

Negative experiments narrow the explanation. They tell future engineers which dimensions have already been controlled and prevent “obvious” but invalid fixes from cycling back into the investigation.

Lecture 13 · Open problems

The last few percent have a different character

1. The 512×8192×4096 pocket

TLX is reproducibly about 2–3% behind local AITER. Both launch 256 workgroups, but their execution shapes differ:

AITER

128×128, four waves, MFMA16, AGPR accumulator, direct A plus pre-shuffled B/scales, deeply hand-interleaved schedule.

TLX

128×128, eight waves, MFMA32, VGPR accumulator, operands/scales staged through LDS, generic wait/read/MFMA/refill ring.

The structurally corrected four-wave clone has the same 256 MFMAs and 136 ds_read_b128 operations as AITER, but still emits 69 waits / 22 barriers versus AITER's 36 / 17. This is now a synchronization and interleaving problem, not a tile-count problem.

2. Reproduce the published AITER baseline

Future reports should record the actual AITER git SHA and dirty state, selected kernel/config, SHA256 of the loaded .co, ROCm/PyTorch versions, clocks/power state, public-wrapper latency, and preallocated kernel-only latency.

3. Compiler opportunities

  • Preserve user-pinned physical layouts robustly through all helper call/return patterns.
  • Make AGPR accumulator selection first-class for scaled MFMA.
  • Factor repeated non-contiguous register bases into legal cooperative transpose reads.
  • Represent LDS overwrite dependencies finely enough to reduce barriers without weakening correctness.
  • Build an instruction scheduler that understands async-copy age, LDS stage ownership, and MFMA consumption together.
Lecture 14 · Transferable lessons

A compact playbook for GPU compiler performance

1 · Reproduce before explaining

Pin source and binaries, alternate runners, flush caches deliberately, and demand exact output.

2 · Fix geometry before micro-scheduling

An underfilled device cannot be repaired by prettier instruction order.

3 · Treat layout as ownership

Logical shape, pointer alignment, per-thread contiguity, and physical distribution are distinct contracts.

4 · Inspect the final ISA

TTGIR can look healthy while LLVM scheduling creates catastrophic scratch traffic.

5 · Make policy local

Tiles, buffer depth, traversal, and scheduler attributes can vary per kernel while one compiler serves all of them.

6 · Preserve negative evidence

A rejected experiment is valuable when it isolates a cause and records its correctness boundary.

Final takeaway: AITER's assembly is not fast because it is assembly. It is fast because it encodes good geometry, physical ownership, dependency distance, and scheduling. TLX becomes competitive when those same ideas are made explicit—and when the compiler preserves them all the way to AMDGPU ISA.
